hook.text: Matcha went from a Zen Buddhist ceremonial drink to a $4 billion global wellness trend in 15 years.

buildup.text: Matcha is shade-grown green tea ground to fine powder — you consume the entire leaf, not just an infusion.

discovery.text: Consuming the whole leaf delivers 10x the antioxidants of regular green tea — plus sustained, calm energy.

twist.text: Most 'matcha' in Western cafés is cooking-grade powder with sugar — ceremonial-grade matcha tastes completely different.

climax.text: Japan can't grow enough to meet global demand. Matcha prices have increased 30% since 2018.

punchline.text: A 900-year-old monk's drink became a latte flavor. Japan is still catching up.

quiz.question: Why does matcha deliver more antioxidants than regular green tea?
options: You consume the entire ground leaf, not just an infusion

details.summary: Matcha is shade-grown green tea ground into fine powder that is whisked whole into water, meaning you consume the entire leaf. Shade-growing increases chlorophyll and L-theanine, producing vibrant green color and a calm alertness.
details.whyItMatters: Matcha's viral global adoption shows how traditional practices can be reinvented for modern markets. Its unique combination of caffeine and L-theanine offers a different stimulation profile than coffee.
takeaways: Shade-growing boosts chlorophyll and L-theanine levels dramatically
Consuming the whole leaf provides more nutrients than steeped tea
L-theanine combined with caffeine produces calm alertness without jitters

faq.question: Why does matcha give a different energy than coffee?
faq.answer: Matcha contains both caffeine and L-theanine, an amino acid that promotes alpha brain waves associated with calm focus. L-theanine slows caffeine absorption, producing a gradual energy rise without the spike and crash of coffee. The combination creates alert relaxation rather than wired stimulation.

faq.question: How can you tell quality matcha from low-grade products?
faq.answer: Ceremonial-grade matcha is vibrant bright green, smells fresh and sweet, and tastes smooth with umami depth. Low-grade matcha is yellowish-brown, smells flat, and tastes bitter. Good matcha comes from the first spring harvest.
